title: Timer row and durable timer kept in step by one activity
source: Recovery Workbench Workflow Engine Design v3, section 4
description: Version 3 keeps every timer as a row in the timer table (E1-028) written through the TimerScheduler port, with JOB-05 as the five-minute check. Architecture v5 (slide 44, JOB-05) retires the check in favour of durable timers inside each workflow, and DP-10 moves the schedule into the owning service. No source states which of the two is authoritative when they disagree, or how a pause, a resume and a cancel are applied to both without a second write path.
evidence: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 4: 'Timers stay rows in the timer table (E1-028)' and 'JOB-05 checks due timers every five minutes and calls the port'. Architecture v5 slide 44, JOB-05: 'durable timers (retired)'. Architecture v5 slide 25: 'Timers that last for years'.
owner_role: Service owner P3 rwb-case with the platform team
proposed: The durable timer is authoritative and the timer row is the audit copy, written by ApplyStateActivity in the same transaction as the state, and read back on a reopen.

title: rwb-platform task queue is not in the 19 services or in the R4 naming rule
source: Recovery Workbench Workflow Engine Design v3, section 5
description: The platform facts of version 3 name three task queues: rwb-case, rwb-integration and rwb-platform. Architecture v5 gives one queue per service (19) and the job map gives JOB-21 and JOB-22 to the platform team but names no queue. R4 of the rules gives a queue only for a service (rwb-<short>), so rwb-platform has no service row, no schema and no owner of record outside the job map.
evidence: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 5, Task queues: 'rwb-case (case workflows, Epic 3+), rwb-integration (multi-step outbound chains, Epic 3+), rwb-platform (smoke and health workflows, Epic 1)'. Architecture v5 slide 24 lists one queue per service; slide 44 gives JOB-21 and JOB-22 to 'platform'. Template and Rules R4 gives a queue per service only.
proposed: Keep rwb-platform as the platform queue of the platform team, outside the 19 service queues, and write it in the Temporal Workflow and Activity Catalog v1.

title: Strict-mode wait at a point of no return is not defined in this design
source: Recovery Workbench Workflow Engine Design v3, sections 3 and 7
description: Version 3 makes the decision log write the gate of the chain and stops the chain when it fails. Architecture v5 records the decision locally in the same transaction as the state change and seals it centrally in rwb-decision, with strict mode at the points of no return. No source states what the workflow does while it waits for the ledger to confirm: whether the activity retries, how long it waits, what the timeout is, and which steps are pivots in workflow terms.
evidence: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 3, WriteDecisionLogActivity: 'This is the gate for the rest of the chain'. Architecture v5 slide 28: 'Strict mode for points of no return ... wait until the central ledger confirms the record'. Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 26 lists the pivots per saga.
owner_role: Service owner P7 rwb-decision with the saga owners S2, S5, S6 and S7
proposed: A pivot activity waits on the ledger acknowledgement with the retry policy of section 7 and a documented timeout, and the workflow fails with an incident when the timeout is reached, without repeating a completed step.

title: Child workflow start policy and failure path are not specified
source: Recovery Workbench Workflow Engine Design v3, sections 3 and 7
description: Version 3 describes one workflow per case and one retry policy for the three case activities. With a child workflow per stage, no source gives the child start-to-close timeout, the parent close policy at every point (only ABANDON for Continue-As-New), the retry of a failed child start, or what the parent does when a child fails after its retries. The gap blocks the Done of every stage story.
evidence: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 7, retry table: 'Initial interval 1 second, Backoff coefficient 2, Maximum attempts 10'. Architecture v5 slide 25 notes: 'Children use parent close policy ABANDON so they survive the parent's Continue-As-New'. No source gives a child failure policy.
owner_role: Service owner P3 rwb-case with the stage owners S1 to S8
proposed: The parent starts the child with the case ID, retries the start with the same workflow ID, and raises an incident with MSG-P3-037 when the retries are exhausted; the case stays in its last applied state.

title: Continue-As-New and a signal that arrives during it
source: Recovery Workbench Workflow Engine Design v3, section 6
description: Version 3 has no Continue-As-New. Architecture v5 sets it at every stage end and at least every 28 days to stay below 51,200 events or 50 MB. No source states how a signal that arrives while a workflow continues as new is held, whether it is delivered to the closing run or the new run, or what happens to a durable timer that is due at that moment.
evidence: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 6 has no Continue-As-New. Architecture v5 slide 25 notes: 'Continue-As-New at every stage end and at least every 28 days keeps each run far below Temporal's limit of 51,200 events or 50 MB'. Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 13: 'Continue-As-New at each stage end, at least every 28 days'.
proposed: The signal handler of the closing run writes the event to the new run before it returns, and a Continue-As-New is triggered only at a stage end, so no event is in flight when the history is cut.

title: Child and kit workflow ID format
source: Recovery Workbench Workflow Engine Design v3, section 5
description: The parent workflow ID is fixed as case-{caseId}. Architecture v5 describes one child workflow per stage and the kit workflows but gives no ID format for either, and no source states whether the case ID prefix is reused or suffixed. The ID is what the UI, the search attributes and the run book of a stage address.
evidence: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 5, Workflow IDs: 'case-{caseId} (for example case-RW-2026-000123); platform-smoke-{yyyymmdd}'. Architecture v5 slide 25 names the children but gives no ID. Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 13 gives none either.
proposed: The parent generates one ID per child from the case ID and the stage code, so a stage can be found from the case ID alone and a restart of the parent cannot create a second child for the same stage.

title: Schedule ID, overlap policy, catch-up window and pause behaviour
source: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1, slide 44
description: The job map gives each job a name, a time and a mechanism, and no more. No source gives the Schedule ID, the overlap policy for a run that is still open, the catch-up window after downtime, the pause-on-failure behaviour, or the retention of a Schedule's closed runs. With nine Schedules and a monthly or six-monthly cadence, each of these changes what a run does.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 44 columns: Job, Name, When, Owner, Mechanism. The Batch and Scheduling Design v4 gives times in Asia/Bangkok and no Schedule attribute. Workflow Engine Design v3 has no Schedules section.
owner_role: Platform team (RWB-PLT-WF) with the owning service
proposed: Name each Schedule after its job ID, allow no overlap, allow no catch-up after downtime, do not pause on failure, and raise the E2-037 alert from the failed run.

title: Workflow kit version, coordinates and compatibility rule
source: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1, slide 23
description: Architecture v5 makes the kit a versioned library with semantic versioning and workers pinned by Worker Versioning, and the rules make RWB-PLT-E1071-CON the dependency of every Schedule and kit user. No source gives the artefact coordinates, the first version number, or the rule that says which kit version a worker build must carry and what happens when a stage service is on a different minor.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 23: 'Kit versioned; workers pinned (Worker Versioning)'. Template and Rules R5.5 DP-10: 'H RWB-PLT-E1071-CON'. Workflow Engine Design v3 has no kit.
proposed: Publish the kit as a versioned library in the service template with a compatibility table per minor version, and fail the build when a worker carries a kit minor that the platform team has not released.

title: Who pauses the stage clock when the stage runs as a child
source: Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1, slide 25, against the parent and child model
description: Architecture v5 says the CaseWorkflow pauses and resumes the stage clock when a deviation arrives, while the stage timer sits inside the stage child on the owner's queue. Version 3 has one workflow, so the question did not arise. No source states whether the parent pauses a clock it does not hold, or instructs the child, and what happens to a child that is started while a deviation is open.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 25 notes: 'DeviationWorkflow (rwb-deviation, can start at any time and pauses the stage clock)'. Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 24 notes: 'the case router delivers DeviationRaised (EV-06) and DeviationCleared (EV-07) to the CaseWorkflow, which pauses and resumes the stage clock'. Workflow Engine Design v3 section 4: 'A deviation pauses the stage clock'.
owner_role: Service owner P3 rwb-case with S8 rwb-deviation
proposed: The parent forwards DeviationRaised to the running stage child, and the child pauses its own stage timer and resumes it on DeviationCleared, so the clock that is paused is the clock that is held.
